overview: Lysimachus built one of the kingdoms that emerged after Alexander the Great’s death. His power began in Thrace and later extended into western Anatolia and Macedonia. The imported map shows mainly Thrace from 300 to 200 BCE. That outline misses much of his later kingdom, and its dates continue long after his death in 281 BCE.

periods.title: A successor becomes king
periods.summary: Lysimachus adopted a royal title and expanded across the straits into Anatolia and Macedonia.

items.text: After the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, Lysimachus gained extensive lands in Asia Minor. He later shared and then took control of Macedonia. His kingdom changed substantially within one lifetime, so a single Thracian outline cannot represent its maximum reach.

Lysimacheia, founded in 309 BCE, bore the king’s name and stood in a strategic position near the Hellespont. After his death, other rulers repeatedly competed for it. A new city could outlast its founder while remaining caught between larger powers.

Across the water in Anatolia, Lysimachus refounded Ephesos around 300 BCE. The project gathered people from nearby smaller settlements into a planned city. The Austrian Archaeological Institute describes the resettlement as forced: a king’s impressive urban project could mean an unwanted move for a household.

Ephesos’s Hellenistic plan included a regular street grid and a fortification circuit about nine kilometres long along the hills. Those surviving walls help identify this early city beneath later building phases. Many famous monuments visible at Ephesos today were rebuilt or added under Rome.

Strabo, writing centuries later, tells an unsettling story about the move: Lysimachus allegedly blocked drains during heavy rain to flood the old settlement and make residents leave. This is an ancient author’s account, not an event established by excavated plumbing. It shows how coercive the king’s reputation could be.

A marble land grant from Cassandreia, dated 285/4 BCE, lists wooded estates and a vineyard given to Limnaios, son of Harpalos. It identifies neighbours as well as areas. Royal property was described through usable resources and local boundaries, not just lines on a grand map.

The same grant allowed Limnaios and his descendants to keep, sell, exchange or give away the estates. This is unusually direct evidence for inherited family wealth under Lysimachus. Such royal favour tells us about a privileged household rather than all rural families.

An Athenian decree credits the poet Philippides with persuading Lysimachus to send 10,000 Attic medimnoi of wheat, distributed to Athenians in 299/8 BCE. A poet at court could do practical diplomatic work. In this case his useful words helped bring grain.

After the battle of Ipsus, Philippides also secured the release of Athenian prisoners. Those who wanted to leave received clothing and travel money from him; others chose further military service. The decree counts more than 300 people helped. It preserves individual choices within a much larger war.

Athens later rewarded Philippides with a bronze statue in the theatre, public dining privileges and a front-row seat at civic competitions. These honours reveal a social world in which poetry, festivals, generosity and royal connections could reinforce one another.

sections.title: A king’s name and another king’s face

items.text: An Otago Museum silver coin minted at Colophon about 299 to 296 BCE reads ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩ[Σ] ΛΥΣΙΜΑΧΟΥ, “of King Lysimachus”. The brackets mark a restored letter in the catalogue’s transcription. This small Greek inscription comes from the Anatolian side of his kingdom, beyond most of the imported outline.

Lysimachus also issued coins showing Alexander with the ram’s horn of the god Amun, while Athena appeared on the reverse. The face was Alexander’s, although the money named Lysimachus. The British Museum explains this as a claim to inherit the conqueror’s prestige.

ending.text: Lysimachus was killed fighting Seleucus at Corupedium in 281 BCE. His Asian lands passed to the Seleucids, while Macedonia entered another struggle for power. His kingdom did not survive intact until the map’s 200 BCE endpoint, although its cities and communities continued.
